definition: Industrial Control System: the computers, controllers and networks that run a physical process such as a gas plant, a power grid or a water works.
Operational Technology: hardware and software that monitors or changes physical equipment. The counterpart of office IT.
Programmable Logic Controller: a rugged industrial computer that reads sensors, runs a control program in a fixed cycle and switches outputs such as motors and valves.
Human-Machine Interface: the screen operators use to watch and control the plant. In CybICS this is FUXA.
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition: the software layer that collects data from many controllers and lets operators supervise a whole site.
A reference model that sorts the devices of a plant into levels, from the physical process (level 0) up to the business network (levels 4 and 5).
The loop a PLC repeats forever: read all inputs, run the program once, write all outputs. CybICS runs it every 50 ms.
Switching on at one value and off at a different one, so a device does not flicker on and off around a single threshold. The CybICS compressor starts below 60 and stops at 90.
The international standard for PLC programming languages, such as Structured Text and Ladder Diagram.
A text-based PLC programming language from IEC 61131-3 that looks a little like Pascal. The CybICS program is written in it.
A simple industrial protocol from 1979. A client asks a server to read or write numbered coils and registers. It has no authentication.
A 16-bit Modbus value that clients can both read and write. CybICS keeps the tank pressures in holding registers 1124 and 1126.
A single on/off value in Modbus, usually an output such as a motor or a valve. On CybICS coil 1 is the compressor.
The byte in a Modbus request that says what to do, for example 03 = read holding registers or 06 = write one register.
Modbus Application Protocol header: the 7 bytes in front of every Modbus TCP message (transaction ID, protocol ID, length, unit ID).
Protocol Data Unit: the part of a message that carries the actual request, after the headers that only transport it.
Siemens' proprietary protocol for its S7 PLCs, carried over TCP port 102 inside TPKT and COTP.
System status list (German: System-Zustandsliste): the self-description an S7 PLC gives on request, including its model and firmware.
A small framing header (RFC 1006) that lets ISO transport messages travel over TCP. S7comm uses it.
Connection-Oriented Transport Protocol (ISO 8073), the transport layer S7comm runs on.
OPC Unified Architecture: a modern industrial protocol with a browsable data model and optional encryption and user authentication.
In OPC-UA, how a connection is protected: not at all (None), signed, or signed and encrypted.
In OPC-UA, how a client says who it is: anonymously, with a username and password, or with a certificate.
Distributed Network Protocol 3, common in electricity and water utilities in North America. OpenPLC serves it on port 20000.
An industrial protocol that carries CIP messages over Ethernet, common with Rockwell/Allen-Bradley PLCs. OpenPLC serves it on port 44818.
Safety Instrumented System: an independent controller whose only job is to bring the plant into a safe state when something goes dangerously wrong.
Gas storage tank: the low-pressure tank of the CybICS plant that feeds the compressor (holding register 1124).
High-pressure tank: the tank the CybICS compressor fills and the consumer draws from (holding register 1126).

The CybICS relief valve. It opens when the HPT pressure goes above 220 bar and closes again when it is back at 200. It vents more slowly than a running compressor fills, so it cannot stop a compressor that is forced on.
Intrusion Detection System: watches network traffic and raises an alert when it matches a rule, such as many Modbus writes from an unexpected host. It does not block anything.
An alert that fires on legitimate activity. Too many of them and operators stop paying attention.
A list of what is permitted; everything else is refused or flagged. The opposite of a blocklist.
A firewall policy that blocks everything that is not explicitly allowed.
Several independent layers of protection, so one failure does not lead straight to an incident.
Splitting a network into separate parts with controlled connections between them, so an intruder in one part cannot reach everything.
In IEC 62443, a group of assets with the same security requirements.
In IEC 62443, the controlled communication path between two zones.
The international family of standards for securing industrial automation and control systems.
Demilitarised zone: a buffer network between the plant and the office network, so neither talks to the other directly.
A public knowledge base of the tactics and techniques attackers use against industrial control systems, each with an ID such as T0846.
In ATT&CK, the attacker's goal at a stage of an attack, such as Discovery or Impair Process Control.
In ATT&CK, a specific way of reaching a tactic's goal, such as Remote System Discovery.
Gathering information about a target before attacking it.
Probing a host's network ports to find which services it runs. nmap is the usual tool.
An attacker who sits between two parties and can read or change everything they send each other.
Sending forged ARP replies so that other hosts send their traffic for an IP address to the attacker's machine.
Sending large amounts of malformed or unexpected input to a program to find crashes and bugs.
Guessing passwords by trying many candidates, often from a wordlist.
Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter: a simple serial interface found on most circuit boards, often left open as a debug console.
A packet capture file, as written by Wireshark or tcpdump.
A free tool that captures network traffic and decodes it protocol by protocol.
A free network scanner that finds hosts and open ports and can identify the services behind them.
The organised way of handling a security incident: prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover and learn from it.
Malware that encrypts a victim's data and demands payment to unlock it.
Hexadecimal: writing numbers in base 16 with the digits 0-9 and A-F. One byte is always two hex digits, from 00 to FF.
Eight bits: a number from 0 to 255, written as two hex digits.
A numbered storage slot in a controller. A Modbus register holds 16 bits, a number from 0 to 65535.
The target value a controller tries to reach, such as the pressure a tank should hold.
A database that records process values over time, for trends, reports and investigations.
The PC an engineer uses to write and download PLC programs. Whoever controls it can change how the plant behaves.
Internet Protocol address: four numbers from 0 to 255, such as 172.18.0.3, that identify a device on a network. Every packet carries the address of its sender and its receiver.
A group of addresses that share the same first part, written like 172.18.0.0/24. Devices on one subnet talk to each other directly; everything else goes through a gateway.
The router a device sends a packet to when the receiver is not on its own subnet. In the CybICS lab network it is 172.18.0.1, the host computer.
A number from 0 to 65535 that says which program on a computer a message is for. Modbus TCP uses 502, OPC-UA 4840.
A small piece of data sent over a network, wrapped in layers that each add addresses: MAC addresses, IP addresses, then ports.
Transmission Control Protocol: opens a connection with a handshake, numbers the packets and resends lost ones, so data arrives complete and in order. Modbus TCP, S7comm and OPC-UA run over it.
User Datagram Protocol: sends single packets without a connection or a delivery check. Faster than TCP, but nothing guarantees a packet arrives.
How TCP opens a connection: the client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, the client confirms with ACK. A SYN-ACK tells a port scanner that a port is open.
Media Access Control address: the hardware name of a network card, six pairs of hex digits such as 02:42:ac:12:00:03. It is only used on the local network segment.
Address Resolution Protocol: a device asks the local network which MAC address belongs to an IP address. Nobody checks the answers, which makes ARP spoofing possible.
A sealed box with its own programs, files and network address that shares the host's operating system. Each CybICS service runs in its own Docker container.
A virtual switch inside the host computer that connects Docker containers. The CybICS containers share the bridge virt-cybics with the subnet 172.18.0.0/24.
A Docker mode in which a container gets no address of its own and uses the host computer's network directly. The CybICS landing page and IDS run this way.
